title: When Will We Ever Use This in Life? The Use of Cognitive Weapons
author: Jo Fujiwara
summary: Jo Fujiwara, a mathematics teacher writing from material in an upcoming book, After the Bell, asks why anyone should learn mathematics once AI can produce the answers. He rejects the common analogy to sport, where robots outrunning humans does not end running, because mathematical reasoning serves purposes beyond the activity itself, from evaluating evidence to catching a bad argument. After surveying recent AI results at the Olympiad level and in research mathematics, he argues that teachers share responsibility, since for decades the answer to when will I ever use this has been applications, which made utility the only reason to think. Drawing on Plato's Phaedrus, Pacific wayfinding and the Naval Academy's dropped and restored celestial navigation, he shows that capacities lapse when nobody needs them, and that stored knowledge is not a skill a person can exercise. He calls mathematical reasoning a cognitive weapon in the sense of a distributed capacity to audit claims and refuse them, and concludes that schools must protect the right to struggle with a question and stop confusing the quality of output with growth.
points: Fujiwara argues that mathematics differs from sport because we depend on reasoning to evaluate evidence, so the risk is a gradual loss of the ability to think independently, not a loss of enjoyment.

He faults teachers for answering when will I ever use this with applications alone, which taught students to ask what thinking will produce and left no reason to think once a machine produces it faster.

Historical examples, from trained memory after writing to Hawaiian navigation and celestial navigation at the Naval Academy, show a capacity lapses quietly when nobody needs it and takes years to rebuild.

His cognitive weapons idea compares independent reasoning to a distributed constitutional safeguard, since you cannot audit claims you cannot compute or contest a model whose assumptions you cannot read.
He describes students who check each step against a solution and mistake arrival at an answer for understanding, and says schools must keep the productive struggle rather than design it away.
quotes: The difference is that mathematics serves a purpose beyond the activity itself. When a machine runs faster than a human, we do not lose our reason to participate in sports. But mathematics is different.
If machines increasingly perform this work for us, the concern is not that people will stop enjoying mathematics. It is that we may gradually lose the motivation and ability to reason independently.

But utility stopped being an illustration and became the reason we offered students the chance to think at all. So students learned to ask what thinking will produce before deciding whether to do any on their own.
The work was completed. Understanding was not necessarily developed. A student can be productive without becoming more capable, and teachers can see that problem even when the grade says otherwise.
Nobody banned it. Nobody needed it after the scroll, so nobody built it, and the training that produced it was allowed to lapse.

These histories are not predictions about what AI will do to mathematics. They show something less dramatic and harder to argue with: knowledge stored somewhere is not the same as a skill a person can exercise.

Reasoning, especially mathematics, plays the same role in verifying claims and defending us against misinformation or technological catastrophes. You cannot audit claims you cannot compute, and you cannot contest a model whose assumptions you cannot read.
The right to struggle with a question is not a punishment we should design away. It is part of how we learn to judge answers, including those supplied by machines.
